finding.claim: reset_password_loose compares the stored reset token to the user-supplied token with loose `==`. An attacker can reset any account's password without knowing the token. If the token arrives as a JSON boolean `true`, `true == 'anystring'` is true. If the stored token is a numeric-looking string such as '0e12345', any other '0e…' numeric string also matches through type juggling. The stored token is not unset or expired after use, so it can also be replayed.
finding.source: $email and $token parameters, which come from the password-reset request. The token can be a non-string type if the body is JSON-decoded.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw = ... WHERE email = $email, at lines 5-6.

trace.note: Loads the stored token for the victim's email.
`$row['token'] == $token` uses loose comparison, so `true` or a '0e' magic-hash string passes.
The password is overwritten, which gives account takeover.

finding.guards_checked: No type cast on $token. No hash_equals, unlike reset_password at line 14. No expiry check and no single-use deletion. The caller is not in the repo, so I could not confirm whether input is cast to string upstream. The function is not called anywhere in this directory, so reachability is unconfirmed.

verdict.guard_found: none in reset.php: there is no cast, hash_equals, expiry or single-use deletion in reset_password_loose. No caller exists in the directory, so any upstream string cast or validation can't be checked.
verdict.reason: The loose `$row['token'] == $token` at reset.php:4 is accurately described and unguarded, and `true == 'str'` passes under PHP 8 type juggling, but reset_password_loose has no callers in the directory (grep found only the definitions at reset.php:2 and :12), so I can't tell whether $token can arrive as a non-string, and the 0e magic-hash case needs a stored 0e-numeric token, which random tokens rarely are.

finding.claim: reset_password compares the token safely with hash_equals, but it never checks token expiry and never invalidates the token after a successful reset. A leaked or intercepted reset token stays valid indefinitely and can be reused to change the password again.
finding.source: $email and $token from the reset request, with a previously issued or leaked token.
finding.sink: UPDATE users SET pw ... at lines 15-16.

trace.note: SELECT token FROM resets WHERE email. It selects no created-at or expiry column.
hash_equals passes whenever the token matches.
The password is updated. There is no DELETE or UPDATE on the resets row afterwards.

finding.guards_checked: hash_equals with a string cast prevents type juggling and timing leaks. The query uses quote(), so there is no SQL injection. I found no expiry or single-use enforcement anywhere in the file. The token generation and the rest of the flow are not in the repo.

verdict.guard_found: hash_equals with (string) cast (reset.php:14) and quote() on SQL (13, 15-16); no expiry check or token invalidation anywhere.
verdict.reason: reset.php:13 selects only `token` (no expiry column), :14 only runs hash_equals, and :15-16 updates the password with no DELETE/UPDATE of the resets row, so a leaked token can be reused indefinitely.
